# 04 · IM, the Interstellar Medium

IM is the machine- and audit-readable intermediary medium in which every CMOS system talks through Milky Way (constitution C1, C2): DMP says
what is meant, IM carries it, CM does it (see the [README](README.md), "Three names, one flow"). This chapter is **IM version 0**: the
encoding, the identities, the token, the envelope, the handshake, one message (the heartbeat), the verify rules and the refusal log.
It is what `Im` encodes and what the verifier in `CM.MilkyWay` checks; chapter [05](05-milky-way.md) says where the verifier
runs. Every section is a draft until the verifier passes its Supernova class on the sandbox; the code and this text change together.

Security context: this chapter is defensive security engineering under the charter in [CHARTER.md](CHARTER.md). It specifies the company's own
entrance and its message check, tested on synthetic data in the sandbox.

## What IM is (the axiomatic chain)

"IM is defined by its ability to make DMP axiomatically sound" (the owner, 2026-10-26). The chain has three links, each defined by the
soundness of the one beneath it: DMP is the axioms; IM is the interface over which a network of nodes that meet DMP is itself a node that
meets DMP; CM is the recipe that makes IM do that (constitution T35). A node is one monolithic stack; a constellation is the same network
as Milky Way one scale down, so the one composition theorem carries from the smallest part to the largest by induction over the scales.

- **The door is what makes it sound.** Every boundary between scales is an IM door: a message passes only with both signatures (C19). A
  node has to keep its guarantee only on what its door let in; behind the door a network keeps it on any input. Proven in the evidence
  chain (`CM.BlackHole/evidence/Dmp/Compose.lean`: `sound`, `galaxy_robust`, `galaxy_is_a_node`, `order_free`), and without the door it
  fails (`echo_alone_not_robust`).
- **No set order where nothing grants.** Modules on one level reference only the stack beneath them and speak only IM, so any arrangement of
  the same modules carries the same guarantees. Edges that carry authority (a grant, a dependency) keep their hierarchy and depth.
- **A version is IM only with its proof.** A version of IM is accepted at a door only when it carries the composition proof for itself,
  checked by both chains (C22); a version without it is refused, so no peer can talk a door down to a version that is not IM.
- **Depth is bounded on the wire (from version 1).** Every envelope carries the depth of its sender in the grant graph (T32), and a door
  refuses a message above the maximum depth, a setting. Version 0 is locked to its fields and carries no depth; there the record bounds it.

What the proof does not yet cover: timing, refusals used as a signal, and inference across nodes; each is a guarantee still to state in
the same shape. Source: `docs/proposals/axiomatic-chain.md`; the owner approved the chain on 2026-10-26 (03:10Z "Approved!", 03:11Z "Yes:
D1 to D18 and the chain").

Status: draft

## What IM version 0 is

IM carries **control data**, never bulk data (bulk data travels by other protocols that Milky Way proxies). Version 0 is the smallest
IM that proves the idea end to end:

1. a **handshake** that lets a device into a session (shared secret, accept, challenge-response, key signing);
2. a **token** signed by Doppler's authority that says who the sender is, which role it is enrolled in, which commands it may send
   and until when;
3. an **envelope** that wraps every message with that token and the sender's own signature, so every message proves itself on its own;
4. the **verify rules**, checked for every message in a fixed order, failing closed;
5. one message kind, the **heartbeat**;
6. the **refusal log**: counts per reason, never content.

Version 0 knows exactly one signature algorithm and one message authentication code (below). There is no negotiation: a sender
cannot ask for a weaker algorithm, and changing an algorithm is a new IM version.

Status: draft

## Transport and ports

From outside, IM reaches Milky Way on **TCP 443** (the one port the provider opens). Inside, every system on our side reaches Milky
Way's internal port **TCP 138** over the VPN; on devices, Doppler's agent owns 138 and blocks NetBIOS there. Nothing on guest or hotel
networks needs to reach Milky Way; laptops away from the office use the VPN. On **both** ports the stream is **TLS 1.3 with a
certificate on each side** before the first IM byte ([05](05-milky-way.md), "Transport encryption"); the VPN on 138 is a second layer,
not a replacement. The listeners themselves are wave 2; the transport they will run is built and tested in the simulator.

On a stream transport each frame is sent as a 4-byte big-endian length followed by the frame. A frame longer than the setting
`milkyway.im.maxFrameBytes` is refused before it is read. The simulator ([05](05-milky-way.md)) passes whole frames in memory, so
no test needs a network.

**What IM version 0 protects and what it does not.** IM protects **authenticity and integrity** of every message (who sent it, that
nobody changed it, that it is fresh and allowed). IM itself does **not** encrypt: confidentiality of control data is the transport's
job, TLS 1.3 on both ports ([05](05-milky-way.md), "Transport encryption"). The verify rules never depend on TLS: a message that
reached the verifier by any path is checked in full. TLS adds confidentiality, keeps devices without a certificate of the new
authority from reaching IM at all, and binds the two identities (the certificate TLS showed is the certificate IM proves).

Status: draft

## Encoding

Every IM structure has one **canonical byte encoding**, so that what is signed is exactly what is sent and there is no second
spelling of the same message. Rules:

- Integers are big-endian: `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, and `i64` for times.
- Times are **Unix milliseconds** (UTC), `i64`.
- `fixed(n)` is exactly `n` bytes. `bytes16` is a `u16` length then the bytes; `bytes32` is a `u32` length then the bytes.
- `id8` is a `u8` length then ASCII. Each field names its alphabet: **name** = `a-z 0-9 . -` (kinds, permissions, roles),
  **subject** = `a-z 0-9 -`, **printable** = bytes `0x21` to `0x7E`. Nothing else is allowed (no Unicode, so no look-alike names).
- A list is a `u8` count then the items. Where a list is a set (permissions), the items are unique and in ascending ordinal order.
- Every structure starts with a three-letter magic and a version byte, and must end exactly where its last field ends: trailing
  bytes, a short field, a length beyond its limit or a character outside its alphabet make the whole frame **malformed**.
- Every signature and every MAC is computed over a **domain tag** (ASCII, then one zero byte) followed by the canonical bytes, so a
  signature made for one purpose can never be replayed as another. The tags of version 0: `IM0/knock`, `IM0/accept`,
  `IM0/response`, `IM0/token`, `IM0/message`.
- Signatures are **ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256**, in the fixed 64-byte IEEE P1363 form (`r || s`), with **low s**: `s` is at most
  half the group order. ECDSA accepts `(r, s)` and `(r, n - s)` alike; IM accepts only the low one, the signer normalises, so a
  signed structure has exactly one valid spelling (invariant I6). MACs are **HMAC-SHA256**. Comparisons of MACs and hashes are
  constant-time.

Limits (version 0): subject 1 to 64, role 1 to 32, kind and permission 1 to 64 characters; at most 16 permissions; a certificate
at most 4096 bytes and a chain at most 4 certificates; a token at most 16 KiB; a payload at most `milkyway.im.maxPayloadBytes`.

Status: draft

## Identities and keys

IM version 0 has four kinds of key, each held by one party and certified by the **new certificate authority** (lane L3; the
sandbox certificate authority of `Im.Trust` stands in for it in every test):

| Key | Held by | Certificate role (EKU) | Signs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Device key | the device (later in its TPM, through Doppler's agent) | `Device` | the handshake response and every message the device sends |
| Gate key | Milky Way's gate | `MilkyWayGate` | the accept frame, so a device knows it talks to the real gate |
| Token signing key | Doppler's authority | `ImTokenSigner` | tokens |
| Root and issuing CA | the certificate authority | (CA) | certificates |

The roles are extended key usages under one private object identifier arc (an ITU-T X.667 UUID arc `2.25.<uuid>`, which needs no
registration), defined once in `Im.Trust`. A certificate whose role does not match its use is refused. A **KeyId** is the
lowercase hex SHA-256 of the certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo; the same KeyId names a device key in Doppler's enrolment.

The **subject** of a token is an opaque identifier that Doppler assigns at enrolment. It is never a host name, a user name or
anything else that identifies the company or a person (constitution C3, C9).

The **shared secret** of the handshake is one value many clients know. It is a gate, not an identity: it keeps casual traffic out
and proves nothing about who is knocking. Identity is the job of the challenge-response and the certificates. The gate accepts the
current secret and the previous one, so the secret can be rotated without a flag day.

Status: draft

## The token

A token says, under Doppler's signature, who the sender is and what it may do. Doppler issues it to an enrolled device; the device
sends it with the handshake and inside every message.

Token body, in this order:

| Field | Encoding | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| magic, version | `"IMT"`, `u8` = 0 | |
| token id | `fixed(16)` | random, names the token in Doppler's records |
| subject | `id8` subject | the opaque device identifier |
| role | `id8` name | the role the device is enrolled in (`laptop`, `server`, ...) |
| subject key id | `fixed(32)` | SHA-256 of the subject key below |
| subject key | `bytes16` | the device's SubjectPublicKeyInfo, ECDSA P-256 |
| permissions | list of `id8` name | the commands it may send, a set (see "Message kinds and permissions") |
| issued at, not before, expires at | `i64` each | Unix milliseconds; `issued at` is for the record, no verify rule reads it (rule 6 bounds `not before` to `expires at`) |
| nonce | `fixed(16)` | random, so two tokens with the same claims never have the same bytes |
| signer chain | list of `bytes16` | the token signing certificate first, then its intermediates; the root need not be sent, and one that is sent earns no trust (the verifier's roots are its own configuration) |

The token on the wire is `bytes32(body)` followed by `fixed(64)` signature, where the signature is made by the token signing key over
`IM0/token` and the body. Doppler calls `ImTokenCodec.Issue` with its `IImSigner`; it decides which permissions a role gets, and a
token's lifetime (`expires at - not before`) is never longer than the setting `milkyway.im.tokenMaxLifetime`.

Status: draft

## The envelope

Every message travels in an envelope. Envelope body, in this order:

| Field | Encoding | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| magic, version | `"IMM"`, `u8` = 0 | |
| kind | `id8` name | which message this is (`im.heartbeat`) |
| message id | `fixed(16)` | random; the replay check keys on it |
| sent at | `i64` | Unix milliseconds, the sender's clock |
| token | `bytes32` | the sender's token, exactly as Doppler issued it |
| payload | `bytes32` | the message itself, encoded as its kind says |

The envelope on the wire is `bytes32(body)` followed by `fixed(64)` signature, made by the **device key named in the token** over
`IM0/message` and the body. Because the token travels inside the signed body, a message cannot be moved to another sender's token,
and because every message carries its token and its own signature, every message verifies itself without any session state
(constitution C2).

Status: draft

## The handshake

The handshake lets a device into a session. It has four steps; each frame starts with a one-byte type.

1. **Knock** (`0x01`, device to gate): `fixed(32)` client nonce, `i64` sent at, `fixed(32)` MAC, where the MAC is HMAC-SHA256 with the
   shared secret over `IM0/knock`, the client nonce and the time. The frame is exactly 73 bytes. The gate checks the length, the
   time (within the clock skew), the MAC against the current and the previous secret, and that the nonce is new. **Any failure gets
   the quiet answer**: no byte back, the connection closed, as a closed firewall port would behave ([05](05-milky-way.md)).
2. **Accept** (`0x02`, gate to device): `fixed(32)` challenge, `fixed(16)` session id, the gate's certificate chain (list of `bytes16`),
   and `fixed(64)` signature by the gate key over `IM0/accept`, SHA-256 of the knock frame, the challenge, the session id and the
   encoded chain. The device checks that the chain validates in the role `MilkyWayGate` and the signature; otherwise it drops the
   connection. This is the gate's half of the key signing: the device knows it talks to the real gate before it shows anything.
3. **Response** (`0x03`, device to gate): the device's certificate chain (list of `bytes16`), its token (`bytes32`), and `fixed(64)`
   signature by the device key over `IM0/response`, SHA-256 of the knock frame, SHA-256 of the accept frame, the encoded chain and the
   token. Signing both earlier frames answers the challenge and binds the response to this one session. The gate checks: the device
   chain validates in the role `Device`; the token passes the token rules (rules 3 to 9 below); the token's subject key id is the
   device certificate's KeyId; the signature is valid; the token carries `im.session.open`.
4. **Established** (`0x04`, gate to device): `fixed(16)` session id. From here the device sends **message** frames (`0x10`, a signed
   envelope); the gate answers each accepted message with **ack** (`0x11`, `fixed(16)` message id).

A failure after a valid knock gets **refused** (`0x7F`, no content) and the gate closes the connection. The refused frame never says
why: the reason is counted, never sent, so the gate is no oracle. A frame of the wrong type for the step, or a handshake that does
not finish within `milkyway.im.handshakeTimeout`, is refused the same way. Inside a session, every message must carry a token for
the session's subject.

Status: draft

## The enrolment door

A machine that is not enrolled yet has no device certificate and no token, so it cannot answer the challenge. The **door** is the
one way such a machine speaks to CMOS, and it reaches **Doppler only**:

1. After a valid knock and the accept (the device has checked the gate, step 2 above) and **before** the response, the device may
   send **door** frames (`0x20`): `bytes32` payload. The gate answers each with a **door reply** (`0x21`): `bytes32` payload.
2. The gate does not read the payload. It passes it to Doppler's door (`Im.IImDoor`, wired in the composition root) and sends
   back what Doppler answers. When Doppler answers nothing, the gate sends **refused** and closes, as for any refusal: the reason is
   counted on Doppler's side and never sent.
3. Nothing from the door is verified, delivered to a consumer or put on the board. The session stays in "waiting for the response";
   the handshake deadline keeps running across the door frames, and at most `milkyway.im.maxDoorFrames` door frames (default 8) of at
   most `milkyway.im.maxDoorBytes` (default 49152) are accepted per session. A door frame in any other state closes the session (before
   the knock: the quiet answer).
4. After the door, the same session may answer the challenge with a token obtained through the door; an enrolled device fetches its
   token this way and opens its session on one connection. On a TLS connection without a client certificate the response is refused
   (`TransportNoCertificate`), so a machine without a certificate can do nothing but use the door.

Refusals of the door, appended to the refusal reasons: `DoorClosed` (the gate has no door), `DoorRefused` (Doppler answered nothing,
or more than the limit), `DoorLimit` (too many door frames). An answered door frame is counted as accepted `DoorFrame`.

**Doppler's payloads.** Doppler owns the payloads; they follow the encoding rules above. A request is `"DPQ"`, version 0, an operation
byte, then its fields; an answer is `"DPA"`, version 0, the same operation byte, then its fields. There is no refusal answer.

| Operation | Request fields | Answer fields |
|---|---|---|
| 1 challenge | none | `fixed(32)` single-use challenge, valid for Doppler's `ChallengeLifetime` |
| 2 enrol begin | `fixed(32)` challenge, `bytes16` endorsement key (SubjectPublicKeyInfo), `bytes16` attestation key (TPMT_PUBLIC) | `fixed(32)` a second single-use challenge, `bytes16` credential blob, `bytes16` encrypted secret (TPM2_MakeCredential to the endorsement key and the attestation key's name) |
| 3 enrol finish | `fixed(32)` the second challenge, `bytes16` the activated credential, the key attestation (`bytes16` device key TPMT_PUBLIC, `bytes16` TPMS_ATTEST of TPM2_Certify, `bytes16` TPMT_SIGNATURE), the PCR 7 quote (`bytes16` TPMS_ATTEST of TPM2_Quote, `bytes16` TPMT_SIGNATURE, `u16` bank, `bytes16` PCR 7, `u16` count then per event `u32` type, `bytes16` digest, `bytes32` data), the reported state (`u8` disk encrypted 0/1, `id8` agent package SHA-256), `bytes16` PKCS#10 request (CM.BlackHole/docs/doppler.md) | `id8` subject, `bytes16` Device certificate, list of `bytes16` chain |
| 4 token | `id8` subject, `fixed(32)` challenge, `bytes16` proof (device-key signature over the token-request statement) | `bytes32` token, `i64` expires at |

The TPM structures inside the fields (TPMT_PUBLIC, TPMS_ATTEST, TPMT_SIGNATURE) are in the TPM 2.0 encoding (big-endian, TPM 2.0
Library Part 2) and the PCR 7 events are the firmware's TCG event records; Doppler parses each strictly.

Doppler bounds what the door can cost it: open challenges are capped (`MaxOpenChallenges`, fails closed when full), a plan is used up by
the enrolment it allows, and every parse failure is counted as `door.malformed` without content.

Status: draft

## Message kinds and permissions

Each kind needs exactly one permission in the sender's token. Version 0:

| Kind | Needs permission | Who gets it (Doppler's policy) |
|---|---|---|
| (handshake) | `im.session.open` | every enrolled role |
| `im.heartbeat` | `im.heartbeat.send` | every enrolled role |

A kind that is not in this table is refused as unknown, even when the token lists a permission of that name. New kinds are added to
this table and to `ImKinds` in the same pull request.

Status: draft

## The heartbeat message

The first and only message of version 0: "this device is alive, and this is its state". It is what Promise B of the laptop lane
shows on the board, marked verified.

Payload: `u8` version = 0, `u64` sequence (counts up per device), `u8` status (0 healthy, 1 degraded, 2 failing; any other value is
malformed), `id8` printable agent version (1 to 32 characters). Nothing else: no host name, no user, no free text.

Status: draft

## The verify rules

The verifier checks every message by these rules, **in this order**, and stops at the first that fails. A message that passes all of
them is **verified**; nothing else reaches a consumer. The rule numbers are referenced by the tests and by the proof work.

| # | Rule | Refusal reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The frame is no longer than `milkyway.im.maxFrameBytes` | `Oversize` |
| 2 | The signed envelope parses strictly (magic, version 0, lengths, alphabets, nothing trailing) | `Malformed`, `UnknownVersion` |
| 3 | The token inside parses strictly; its subject key is ECDSA P-256 and its SHA-256 is the subject key id | `Malformed`, `UnknownVersion` |
| 4 | The token's signer chain validates to a trusted root in the role `ImTokenSigner` at the verifier's time | `UntrustedTokenSigner`, `CertificateExpired` |
| 5 | The token signature is valid under the signer certificate's key | `BadTokenSignature` |
| 6 | The token's lifetime is at most `milkyway.im.tokenMaxLifetime`, and `not before <= expires at` | `TokenPolicy` |
| 7 | Now is not before `not before` minus the clock skew | `TokenNotYetValid` |
| 8 | Now is before `expires at` (no skew on expiry) | `TokenExpired` |
| 9 | Doppler's enrolment knows the subject, has not revoked it, and holds the same role and key id | `NotEnrolled`, `Revoked`, `EnrolmentMismatch` |
| 10 | Inside a session: the token's subject is the session's subject | `SessionMismatch` |
| 11 | The envelope signature is valid under the token's subject key | `BadMessageSignature` |
| 12 | `sent at` is within the clock skew of now, both ways | `Stale` |
| 13 | The kind is in the table of kinds | `UnknownKind` |
| 14 | The token carries the permission the kind needs | `WrongPermission` |
| 15 | The payload parses strictly as its kind says | `Malformed`, `UnknownVersion` |
| 16 | The pair (subject key id, message id) has not been seen; it is remembered until `sent at` plus the clock skew | `Replayed`, `ReplayCacheFull` |

Why this order: cheap structural checks first, so garbage costs nothing; the authority's signature before anything that trusts the
token's contents; the sender's signature before the replay check, so nobody can fill the replay memory with messages they cannot
sign; the replay check last, so a refused message never uses up an id. Why rule 16 is complete: an id is forgotten only once its
`sent at` is more than the skew in the past, and from then on rule 12 refuses the message anyway. When the replay memory is full and
nothing in it has expired, the verifier refuses (fails closed) rather than forget early.

The verifier has no other way to accept: there is no debug switch, no allow list and no "trusted network" that skips a rule.

Status: draft

## The refusal log

Every refusal is **counted by reason**, and every accepted message by kind. The log takes nothing else: its interface accepts only the
reason and the kind as enumerations, so no subject, no token, no payload, no address and no secret can reach it by construction
(a test checks the interface). It is what CMB reads later ("counts, never content"). Exceptions inside the verifier are counted as
`Malformed` and never carry the frame into a message.

Status: draft

## Invariants for proving

The statements the tests prove now and that Singularity's proofs (Gravity down from DMP, Lean up from the C#; draft, DMP 0.9.0) and the Supernova
level take over later. Each is a test in the `im` group today.

- **I1, verified implies authorised.** A message is verified only if a token signed by a trusted `ImTokenSigner` names an enrolled,
  unrevoked subject whose key signed the message, and the token is in its validity window and carries the kind's permission.
- **I2, no replay inside the window.** The same signed message is verified at most once.
- **I3, the log carries no content.** The refusal log's interface admits only enumerations.
- **I4, no algorithm choice.** Version 0 parses only ECDSA P-256 keys and 64-byte signatures; anything else is malformed.
- **I5, the quiet answer.** Before a valid knock the gate sends no byte.
- **I6, canonical form.** Parsing then encoding returns the same bytes; any other bytes do not parse.

Assumptions the proof work must turn into runtime checks or Supernova tests: the transport provides confidentiality (now a test: on
the simulator's wire neither the token, the payload nor the device certificate appears in clear); the verifier's clock is right within
the skew; the private keys stay where they are held; the enrolment registry tells the truth. Two more came out of the GRB-0001 run
(2026-10-25). Rule 4 trusts the role, not one key: any `ImTokenSigner` certificate of the new authority signs tokens the gate accepts,
so the issuing CA endpoint is inside the verifier's decision (only Doppler may request that role; Doppler's watch alarms on an accepted
token id it did not issue). The device certificate is checked at the handshake only; a session outlives a certificate that expires or is
revoked in it by at most the token's lifetime, and rule 9 reads the enrolment for every message. The assumption audit of the verifier
(chapter 06, class IIb) lists each one with the check or test that carries it: `CM.MilkyWay/docs/supernova/assumptions.md`.

Status: draft

## What is not in IM version 0

Wave 2 and later, each a new section here when it is built: the listeners on TCP 443 and 138 in the DMZ (the TLS they run is built,
chapter 05); commands beyond the heartbeat and the permission model for
them; revocation of a signing certificate through a published list (in version 0 a signing certificate is revoked by removing it
from the trust configuration, a device by Doppler's enrolment); the shield's classes and tokens on values (chapter 05, MW0); rate limits per subject (the limit on connections at once and the deadlines are built, chapter 05 "Resource limits"), and a cache
of chain verdicts so a busy gate does not rebuild the same chain for every message; the galaxy group (federated Milky Ways).

## Compatibility after the lock

Constitution C18: once the first productive system speaks IM, the version it speaks is locked (`DMP/im-lock.txt`) and IM stays
backwards compatible for good. Consequences for every version still being designed (version 1 above all): leave room to add message
kinds, permissions and optional parts without a new wire for the old ones, because after the lock nothing can be taken back. The rule
"a gate runs exactly one version, no negotiation" holds until the first lock; how a gate accepts a locked version next to a newer one
without opening a downgrade is designed in the version that comes after the lock. The corpus of a locked version holds its messages with
the trust anchors and the verify time they were captured with, so tokens that have expired since still replay.

**When a locked algorithm becomes unsafe** (C18, the owner, 2026-10-25): the locked version is not retired. Milky Way keeps speaking it,
weak algorithm included, to every system locked to it, and moves that system onto a contained path: the path is Milky Way's own (the
system reaches nothing else and nothing reaches it except through Milky Way); what arrives on it is not trusted for what the weak
algorithm claims, so the proof of origin comes from the path, not from the signature; and Milky Way re-signs what it forwards under a
current version with no more rights than the locked system had. To design before the first lock: how the path proves origin (TLS on
a current algorithm under the weak IM, a per-device port, the TPM), and how the gate marks a contained system in its counters.

Status: draft

## IM version 1: two chains of trust (proposal)

Not built. This section proposes IM version 1 so that the Black Hole CA plan (`CM.BlackHole/docs/ca-plan.md` sections 1a and 1b) and
Milky Way build against one text. It was agreed between the Milky Way and the Black Hole lanes on 2026-10-25. Where it differs from
version 0, version 1 wins once it is built; until then version 0 is what the code does. Version 0 stays in the sandbox and never
reaches a real network. A gate runs exactly **one** version, and there is no negotiation between versions (I4 holds across versions,
not only inside one).

**Why a new version.** Every Milky Way component is admitted only while six checks hold, three for each of two independent chains
(ca-plan 1a): its leaf is signed by the chain's issuing CA, the chain validates to that chain's root in the right role, and that
chain's master accepts the component in its register with a valid token.

- The **security chain** belongs to Doppler, which attests "this machine is what it claims and is healthy now".
- The **operational chain** belongs to the operations master, which attests "this machine is supposed to exist, in this role".

Version 0 carries one chain and one token, so it cannot express this.

**What stays as in version 0:**

- the encoding;
- the knock and the quiet answer;
- the frame types and their order;
- ECDSA P-256 with low s and HMAC-SHA256 (both token signers are P-256; the two chains differ in algorithm family only at the
  CA level, ca-plan section 5);
- the refusal frame without content;
- the replay rule;
- the resource limits.

The domain tags become `IM1/...`, so a version 0 signature never verifies as version 1. Every magic carries version 1.

**One key, two leaves, two tokens.**

- A component has one device key, generated in its TPM.
- It holds **two certificates for that key**: a security leaf in the role `Device` under the security root, and an operational leaf
  in the role `Device` under the operational root. Their SubjectPublicKeyInfo must be byte-identical (`Im.Trust.DualTrust`), so
  one signature proves possession for both.
- TLS carries only the security leaf, as in version 0 ("TLS binding" in [05](05-milky-way.md)). The operational leaf travels inside IM.
- It holds **two tokens** in the version 0 layout plus one field, `authority` (`u8`: 1 = security, 2 = operational), placed right after
  the version, so a token cannot be presented in the other slot.
  - The security token is signed by Doppler's token signer, in the role `ImTokenSigner` under the security root.
  - The operational token is signed by the operations master's token signer, in the role `ImTokenSigner` under the operational root.
  - Each chain validates against its own anchors only. A root configured for both chains is refused (`DualTrust.Over`).
- Both tokens name the same subject and the same subject key id. The component may send a kind only when **both** tokens carry its
  permission (the intersection).

**Frames that change:**

- **Response** (`0x03`) carries the device's security chain, its operational chain, the security token and the operational token,
  in this order, then one signature by the device key over `IM1/response`, the two frame hashes and those four fields.
- **Envelope** (`"IMM"`, version 1) carries both tokens in place of one (security, then operational). The device key signs over
  `IM1/message`.
- **Accept** (`0x02`) carries both of the gate's chains (security, then operational), signed once by the gate key over `IM1/accept`.
  The gate is a Milky Way component too, so the six checks apply to it: the device runs `DualTrust` on the two gate chains and
  drops the connection unless both validate in the role `MilkyWayGate` with the same SubjectPublicKeyInfo. A gate that only one
  master vouches for cannot take devices.
- Established, message, ack, refused, the door and the door reply keep their shape.

**Verify rules.**

- Rules 1 and 2 stay.
- Rules 3 to 9 run **once per chain**, security first, then operational. Each runs against that chain's anchors, its pinned
  token-signer key ids (which closes assumption A14 for version 1) and its master's register: Doppler's enrolment for security,
  the operations master's inventory register for operational.
- A new rule follows: the two tokens name the same subject, role and subject key id. Its refusal is `ChainMismatch`.
- Rules 10 to 16 stay, with one change: rule 14 needs the permission in both tokens.
- The order is still cheap first and fail closed. A component that fails any of the six checks is refused at its next message, because
  every message carries both tokens.

**Refusal log.** Each refusal is counted by (reason, chain), where chain is `none` (structure, replay, session), `security` or
`operational`. The log still takes only enumerations (I3).

**The isolated state.** A gate is in one of two states: **open** (as version 0) or **isolated**.

- While isolated, the gate gives every knock the quiet answer, counted as `Isolated`. It ends every established session with
  refused, counted as `SessionEndedIsolated`.
- Doppler isolates the gate as part of its security isolation (ca-plan 1b: nothing gets out). The gate enters the state on one of two
  inputs:
  - an **isolation order** that it verifies;
  - its own evidence that the security master's trust is broken: Doppler's signed health report is refused, or Doppler's chain no
    longer validates.
- **Silence alone** (a stale health report) raises an alarm and never isolates (Q6, decided by the owner 2026-10-25): isolating on
  silence would hand anyone who can cut a cable a switch that shuts the company down.

**Orders and the White Key.** The **White Key** is the cold-start key (lane L10) in its role as the override: a hardware token with a
PIN, in three copies, any one enough (ca-plan 1b). Whoever holds a White Key settles what the two masters cannot settle between them.

- An order is a signed statement with these fields:
  - magic `"IMO"` and version 1;
  - `u8` kind (1 = isolate, 2 = lift, 3 = pick a winner, 4 = override);
  - `u8` scope (1 = security, 2 = operational);
  - `fixed(16)` order id;
  - `i64` issued at;
  - `id8` reason name.
- The order body is followed by a list of one or two signatures, each a `fixed(32)` signer key id and a `fixed(64)` signature over
  `IM1/order` and the body. Two signatures must come from two different keys.
- An **isolate** order verifies under Doppler's security leaf or under a White Key. Every other kind verifies **only under a White
  Key**, checked against the pinned public keys in the gate's settings (`milkyway.im.whiteKeys`, never fetched):
  - **lift** ends one isolation, the one its scope names;
  - **pick a winner** settles a split brain (both masters alive, each distrusting the other): the scope names the chain to keep, and
    the other master rebuilds its trust from it. This is a permanent write, and a White Key holder is never the single origin of
    trust for one (the owner, 2026-10-25), so it needs **two** signatures: a White Key and either the winning master's leaf or a
    second, different White Key;
  - **override** lifts both isolations as they stand.
- Isolate, lift and override are reversible and need one signature. A White Key holder may read everything while the key exists,
  but never writes permanently alone (whether "permanent" is read this way is the owner's Q7 on #67; the order shape fits either
  reading).
- Nothing else ends an isolation: there is no timeout and no automatic recovery. In a split brain neither master outranks the other,
  and both stay isolated until a White Key order settles it.
- White Keys are ECDSA P-256 like every other IM signature, so IM keeps one algorithm; hardware tokens that speak PIV support it.
- Orders are replay-checked by order id, refused outside the clock skew, and counted by kind and outcome. An accepted lift is
  announced through the health report, so the holders of the other White Key copies see it.
- An order's validity is in its signature, not its path, so any path may carry it: a message kind from Doppler, and a console path
  that must always work, because a lift is needed exactly when the network path may be closed.

**Supernova.** Version 1 changes the decision code, so the version 0 evidence (refusal suite, mutation, fuzzing, GRB-0001) does not carry
over. Version 1 needs class IIn from scratch, with a new GRB scope file. The isolation decision decides what may leave and enter, so it
is class IIb (ca-plan 1b). The rollout follows ca-plan 1b:

1. "would isolate": alarms only;
2. enforcement on the sandbox, with a GRB run against the triggers;
3. enforcement in production, on the owner's words only.

**Settled with the Black Hole lane and the owner (2026-10-25):** the gate shows both chains; orders take any path; White Keys are
P-256; isolation never starts on silence (Q6). The algorithm families of the two chains differ at the CA level (ca-plan section 5).

Status: draft

## Serving at a warehouse (proposal)

Not built. Constitution C19 (the owner, 2026-10-25) says an information warehouse serves an IM request only when it carries a Doppler
signature and an operations-master signature, each from the master or from an authority the other master co-signed. IM version 1 already carries
most of this: the request is an envelope signed by the device key, and its two tokens are the two masters' grants to that device, so a
version 1 envelope proves both chains. C19 adds three things:

- **End to end.** The warehouse runs verify rules 3 to 9 for both chains, the `ChainMismatch` rule and the intersection of permissions
  itself, on every request, against anchors and token-signer key ids pinned in its own settings. It never takes a "verified" mark from
  Milky Way or the operations master. The tokens are the delegation, so serving never needs a live call to either master.
- **Co-signed authorities.** Every authority that signs on a master's behalf (today the two token signers in the role `ImTokenSigner`,
  later any authority that may grant that right) holds certificates for one key under both roots, as a device does (`DualTrust`): its
  own chain in the role `ImTokenSigner`, and the other master's certificate for the same SubjectPublicKeyInfo. A token whose signer
  lacks the other chain's certificate is refused as `GrantNotCosigned`. The two tokens of one request are signed by two different keys,
  so one stolen signer key never mints both.
- **Registered.** A warehouse that serves IM is listed in `DMP/warehouses.txt` as `yes` and has a test that proves the refusals
  (missing security token, missing operational token, a signer only one master certified, the same key behind both tokens); DMP-016
  checks both.

Open design items: the role name the other master uses when it co-signs a signer; whether a "cluster" signs with one key or each node
with its own; how a revoked co-signature reaches a warehouse that serves offline.
